terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, with an accusative and infinitive or a question
evidence: Cic. Att. 14.21.1: cito conjēcī Lānuvī tē fuisse
terms.comment: Literally “throw together”: to put two and two together. Ut conjiciō, at a guess (Ter. Heaut. 63).

evidence: Cic. Att. 14.22.1: nē nihil conjectūrā aberrem
M-O s.v. guess right, guess wrong
terms.comment: Conjectūram facere, to make a guess (Plaut., Ter., Cic.: Lewis & Short); conjectūrā assequī, to guess right, and conjectūrā aberrāre, to guess wrong (M-O).

evidence: Cic. Att. 16.8.2: nōn equidem hoc dīvīnāvī

terms.register: vōx cōmica hōc sēnsū: Plaut., Ter.
evidence: Ter. Ad. 202: sed ego hoc hariolor
M-O s.v. guess: make a wild guess
terms.comment: Properly “prophesy” (Cic. Div. 1.132); “talk nonsense, be dreaming” in comedy (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: a rough idea, a rough guess
evidence: Traupman p. 107: rough guess, īnfōrmāta cōgitātiō
terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase, “a thought sketched in outline”; Lewis & Short does not quote it. For a guess, conjectūra is the word.

phrases.latin: annōs sexāgintā nātus es aut plūs eō, ut conjiciō
phrases.english: you are sixty or more, I’d guess

phrases.latin: sed cito conjēcī Lānuvī tē fuisse
phrases.english: but I soon guessed that you had been at Lanuvium

phrases.latin: nōn equidem hoc dīvīnāvī sed aliquid tāle putāvī fore
phrases.english: I certainly did not guess this, but I did think something of the kind would happen

sources: Lewis & Short: conicio · Lewis & Short: conjectura · Lewis & Short: divino · Lewis & Short: hariolor
